name: Lübeck
title: Lübeck-Travemünde Ferry and Ro-Ro Thickness Gauging
description: Thickness gauging in Lübeck and Travemünde for Finland and Sweden ro-pax ferries, forest-product ro-ro ships and feeders: car decks, ice belt and piping.
h1: UTM for Ro-Pax Ferries, Ro-Ro Ships and Feeders in Lübeck and Travemünde
intro: Lübeck's port stretches along the River Trave from the Skandinavienkai at Travemünde to terminals near the old city, and most of its trade rolls on wheels: ro-pax ferries to Finland, Sweden and Latvia, ro-ro ships carrying paper and forest products, and container feeders. Many of these ships spend the winter in Baltic ice and the rest of the year on fixed rotations. Superintendents use a Travemünde call to gauge decks, ice-belt structure and piping, and each time the technicians are sent out from India to meet the ship.

highlights.p: Ships on the Helsinki route spend weeks each winter forcing through ice in the Gulf of Finland. After the ice season, gauging the ice-belt plating and frames from inside the wing tanks shows how much abrasion and denting the winter has added.

Ro-pax and ro-ro ships at Travemünde load heavy trailers and cassettes on every call. Main-deck and lower-hold plating, ramp hinges and lashing-socket areas take that wear, and can be gauged and crack-checked when lanes are clear.

Paper reels and sawn timber arrive from Finland and Sweden on ro-ro and con-ro ships at the river terminals. Those ships often lie longer than the ferries, giving time to open ballast tanks and void spaces for gauging.

port.h: Lübeck and Travemünde: the port along the Trave
p: Lübeck is a river port. The city stands some way inland on the Trave, and the river runs north-east to the Baltic at Travemünde, where the Skandinavienkai, the port's main ferry and ro-ro terminal, faces the open water of Lübeck Bay. Between the two, terminals line the river banks: the Nordlandkai and other quays nearer the city handle forest products, steel and general cargo, and a container terminal serves Baltic feeders. The Lübecker Hafen-Gesellschaft runs most of these terminals. Ships heading upriver pass Travemünde's waterfront, the Priwall peninsula and the old four-masted barque Passat, now a museum ship, before the river narrows towards the city. The approach is sheltered and tidal range is small, so the river matters more for its width and depth than for any lock.

The ferry network ties Lübeck to the north and east. Finnlines runs ro-pax ships to Helsinki and to Malmö, TT-Line links Travemünde with Trelleborg, and Stena Line sails to Liepāja in Latvia. The Helsinki ships are large, ice-strengthened vessels that carry freight trailers as their main business, with passengers alongside. The Swedish services run frequently, with more than one sailing a day on the busier links, and carry mostly trucks and trailers. Beyond the ferries, ro-ro and con-ro ships bring paper, pulp and sawn timber from Finnish and Swedish mills for distribution across Germany and central Europe, and container feeders connect Lübeck with the large hubs and with other Baltic ports. Cruise calls at Travemünde are fewer than at Kiel or Warnemünde, but smaller cruise ships do visit in summer.

That mix shapes the inspection work. Ferries on the Swedish routes turn around in a few hours and rarely stand idle, so in-service gauging focuses on systems and spaces the crew can release, while hull programmes wait for the refit. The Helsinki ships have a longer stay at Travemünde between their crossings, and once winter navigation in the Gulf of Finland is over, owners want to know what the ice has done to shell plating and frames. Forest-product ro-ro ships often lie at the river terminals for a day or more while cassettes and paper reels are discharged, which gives better access to ballast tanks and voids. Feeders bring short, targeted jobs on scrubber lines and deck plating, usually requested by a manager who has seen wastage noted in a recent report.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged in Lübeck and Travemünde
p: The Skandinavienkai is where most ferry gauging happens. A ro-pax ship there is alongside a linkspan with cargo moving across its decks, so the team works in spaces away from the traffic, such as engine-room piping, sea water inlet lines, voids and tanks the crew can empty, and steps onto the vehicle decks only when the lanes have cleared. Lübeck has no commercial drydock for ships of this size, and the ferries and ro-ro ships calling here dock at yards in Poland, Denmark, Finland or elsewhere. Gauging at Travemünde before such a docking lets the superintendent arrive at the yard with a steel estimate already prepared.

The river terminals give longer, quieter windows. Ro-ro ships discharging forest products at the Nordlandkai and neighbouring quays can release ballast tanks and voids for gauging while cargo work continues on deck, and ships waiting for a berth or for their next sailing lie at lay-by quays on the Trave. Container feeders at the city terminal are measured during short calls for specific items. Ships at anchor in Lübeck Bay are reached by launch for small scopes when the weather allows boarding.
list: Skandinavienkai, Travemünde — engine-room piping, voids, tanks and vehicle-deck plating on ro-pax ferries to Finland, Sweden and Latvia.
Nordlandkai and other river quays — ballast tank, void and lower-hold gauging on forest-product ro-ro and con-ro ships during discharge.
Container terminal in the city port — scrubber wash-water lines, deck plating and hatch covers on Baltic feeders during short calls.
Lay-by quays along the Trave — longer programmes on ferries out of service, ships awaiting charter and vessels for sale.
Lübeck Bay anchorage — small, pre-planned scopes by launch when the ship is waiting to enter the river.

context.h: Ro-pax rules, winter navigation and port state control
p: Ro-pax ferries in regular service from Lübeck are inspected under Directive (EU) 2017/2110, which requires pre-commencement and regular inspections of ro-ro passenger ships by the host state, on top of class surveys and Paris MoU port state control. German inspections are carried out by the Ship Safety Division of BG Verkehr. Fire mains, sea water systems, bilge piping and the structure around bow and stern doors are among the items those inspections follow closely. An operator with recent wall-thickness readings on those systems is in a stronger position when inspectors or the flag state ask how the ship's piping has aged.

The Finnish routes add winter navigation. Finnish and Swedish authorities set ice-class and minimum-size restrictions for ports in the northern Baltic each winter, and the Finnish-Swedish ice class rules determine how a ship's ice belt is built. Shell plating and framing there wear faster than elsewhere on the hull, from abrasion and repeated contact with ice. Ferry operators on these routes also carry the weight of EU emissions rules on frequent, fuel-intensive crossings, with the ETS since 2024 and FuelEU Maritime since 2025, while the EU Ship Recycling Regulation obliges every ship calling at an EU port, whatever its flag, to keep an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs at Lübeck and Travemünde
jobs.p: Work in Lübeck follows the ferry timetable and the forest-product trade. Most ferry jobs are defined lists of piping and tank work done during the port stay, with hull structure scoped for the refit, while ro-ro ships at the river terminals offer the time for ballast tanks and voids. After the ice season, owners of ice-class ships often add shell plating and frames in the ice belt. Each scope is agreed with the chief engineer or chief officer before arrival, so that the crew can release spaces in a known order and the readings reach the superintendent before departure. Examples:
list: A Helsinki-route ro-pax ship in spring: ice-belt plating and frames gauged from inside the wing tanks during its stay at the Skandinavienkai.
A Trelleborg-route ferry during its port stay: fire main and sea water cooling lines measured in the engine room, reported before departure.
A forest-product ro-ro ship discharging paper reels at a river terminal: ballast tanks, voids and lower-hold plating gauged while cassettes move on deck.
A Baltic container feeder at the city terminal: scrubber wash-water and overboard lines measured with the system off, plus hatch-cover panel readings.
A ro-pax ferry before its refit: main-deck plating, ramp hinges and bow-door surroundings gauged and crack-checked to prepare the yard's steel list.

logistics: Hamburg Airport is the usual international arrival point, with road and rail connections to Lübeck and a local rail line on to Travemünde. The ferry and ro-ro terminals are ISPS-controlled, and on passenger ships the team's boarding is aligned with the ship's security plan; the agent registers names and equipment in advance. The technicians travel from India on Schengen visas, and because the ferry timetables are published well ahead, a mobilisation date can usually be fixed early and kept.

faqs.q: Can a Finland-route ferry be gauged at Travemünde without missing a sailing?
faqs.a: For piping, voids and tanks that the crew can release during the port stay, yes. The longer lay-over between Helsinki crossings gives more room than the frequent Swedish services do. Large hull and car-deck programmes for a renewal survey still need the refit, when the ship is out of service and staging is available, but in-service readings help define that scope.

faqs.q: What should be gauged after a winter in the Baltic ice?
faqs.a: The ice-belt shell plating fore and aft, the frames and stringers behind it, and the bow area, measured from inside the wing tanks and forward spaces. Readings are compared with the original thickness and with the previous survey, and dents or deformed frames are recorded on the sketch. Doing this in spring gives the owner time to plan repairs before the next ice season.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Lübeck or Travemünde?
faqs.a: Not for ships of ferry or ro-ro size. Ships calling here usually dock at yards in Poland, Denmark, Finland or elsewhere, chosen by the operator. Gauging at Travemünde or at the river terminals is done afloat, and the readings, referenced to frames and strakes, can be passed to the docking yard and the class surveyor ahead of the docking.

faqs.q: Can ballast tanks be gauged on a ro-ro ship while it discharges paper?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Ballast tanks and voids sit below and beside the cargo decks and can be entered while cassettes and paper reels move above, provided the crew has emptied and ventilated them and the ship's permit system allows entry during cargo work. Lower-hold plating is measured once that hold is clear. The order of spaces is agreed with the chief officer before arrival.

faqs.q: Which Travemünde terminal will the team need to reach?
faqs.a: Ferries use the Skandinavienkai at Travemünde, while forest-product ro-ro ships and feeders use quays further upriver towards the city. The agent confirms the berth and arranges ISPS access for the right terminal, and the team plans its arrival accordingly. If a ship moves between berths during its stay, the scope is split so that each part is done where access is easiest.
